title: Value, price, and the NPV rule
hook: Would you pay $100,000 today for $105,000 next year? The answer hangs on one number the bank already knows.
objectives: Explain the difference between price and value, and why value is only an estimate.
Apply the NPV decision rule: invest when NPV is positive, reject when it is negative.
Discount a future cash flow to the present and see how the discount rate moves the answer.

blocks.md:
Price is what the market charges today. **Value** is what you calculate: the discounted future cash flows an asset will produce.

> "Value is what we're going to calculate. It's a quantitative calculation. Price is just price."

In the long run they meet. In the short run, price swings by billions a day while true value barely moves.

rows.label: What it is
cells: What the market charges right now
A calculated estimate: discounted future cash flows, i.e. NPV

rows.label: Precision
cells: An estimate. Extra decimals are an illusion

rows.label: Moves with
cells: Interest rates and revised cash-flow forecasts

rows.label: Who acts on the gap
cells: Value investors (Buffett, Ackman, Marks) buy when price is well below value

blocks.text: Buffett's intrinsic value is the discounted cash that can be taken out of a business over its remaining life. That is net present value.

blocks.q: A stock's value is $100 and you are 99% sure. It trades at $98. Why might a value investor still pass?
options: Value and price are the same thing
$2 of upside is too thin to cover the chance your estimate is wrong
Prices above value are always better buys
Value estimates are exact, so there is no risk
blocks.why: That is the margin of safety. The lecture's version: Buffett may wait for $80 or $60 on something he thinks is worth $100, because even he might be wrong.

steps.title: Market prices and the bucket of cash

blocks.md:
When you cost something out, use the **market price**, not what it is worth to you. A $4 coffee that is worth $15 to you still goes in the model at $4.

That makes some decisions trivial. NPV is *"a bucket of cash today"*: positive means you receive that much, negative means you give it away.

frames.title: The offer
frames.text: You can buy 200 barrels of oil and 3,000 pounds of copper for $12,000.

frames.title: Price the pieces at market
frames.text: Oil trades at $50 a barrel, copper at about $2 a pound. Whether your firm needs them is irrelevant: sell what you do not use.

frames.title: Translate the offer
frames.text: Strip the story away. Would you hand over $12,000 to receive $16,000?

frames.title: Read the bucket
frames.text: NPV is positive, so take it. Done.

blocks.text: Positive NPV: invest. Negative NPV: reject. Whether prices feel fair, or whether you personally need the goods, does not enter.

blocks.q: Your firm has no use for oil. Does that change the decision to buy the $16,000 basket for $12,000?
options: Yes, you would be stuck with useless inventory
No, you sell what you do not need at market, so the $4,000 NPV stands
Yes, you must first forecast future oil prices
No, but only if you keep the oil
blocks.why: The professor's point: you take what you need and sell the rest. The future price is not part of this question.

steps.title: Why a later dollar is worth less

blocks.md:
Would you pay $1,000 for $1,000 handed over after class? Almost. For $1,000 on Wednesday, a bit less: counterparty risk. Next January, less again. In 2050, a lot less, because inflation shrinks what $1,000 buys.

> "Most people have never heard of that phrase out in the world. But they're doing it all the time."

blocks.prompt: Order these $1,000 payouts from the one you would pay the most for to the one you would pay the least for.
blocks.why: Each step out adds risk (the payer disappears, a COVID-style shock) and, far out, inflation. So the price you would pay today falls with distance.

blocks.title: Present value of $1,000 at a 7% rate
blocks.caption: PV = 1,000 / 1.07^t, one flat rate for every horizon. Illustration, not from the slides.

blocks.md:
The offer: pay **$100,000** now, receive **$105,000** in a year. The market rate is 7%, so safe money grows to $107,000. Does 105 beat 107?

> "If I came to you and said, would you like to destroy $2,000? I think it's clear."

frames.title: Grow today's cash forward
frames.text: Put the $100,000 in the bank at 7% instead.

frames.title: Compare in year-1 dollars
frames.text: The offer pays only $105,000. You are $2,000 behind.

frames.title: Or discount the payoff back
frames.text: Divide the future cash by (1 + r) to see what it is worth today.

frames.title: Same verdict today
frames.text: You are paying $100,000 for something worth $98,131.

blocks.text: The decision does not change with the date you measure it. Minus $2,000 in a year or minus $1,869 today: both say reject.

blocks.q: Same offer, but the discount rate is 4% instead of 7%. What happens to the PV of the $105,000?
options: It falls below $98,130
It rises to about $100,962, so NPV turns positive
It stays the same
It becomes negative
blocks.why: A lower rate means a smaller discount: 105,000 / 1.04 = 100,961.54, so NPV is about +$962.

steps.title: NPV is a curve in the discount rate

blocks.md:
Drag the rate. NPV falls as the rate rises and crosses zero at exactly 5%, where $100,000 grows to $105,000. The world piles risk premiums on top of the risk-free rate, so a riskier version of this deal might use 11%.

> "You want me to take on more risk? I need a better value, better price, in other words."

blocks.title: NPV of paying $100,000 for $105,000 in one year
blocks.caption: At 7% the deal destroys $1,869 today. Break-even is 5%.

blocks.q: A copier costs $9,500 today, or $10,000 in a year. The rate is 7%. Which is the better deal?
options: Pay $9,500 now, it is cheaper on the sticker
Pay $10,000 in a year: that is worth $9,345.79 today, about $154 less
They are identical
You cannot tell without forecasting copier prices
blocks.why: 10,000 / 1.07 = 9,345.79. Paying later saves about $154 in today's dollars, assuming the 7% rate is right (a big assumption).

steps.title: Too many good projects: take the biggest bucket

blocks.md:
You are a student who started a web-hosting business. An investor will buy it for $200,000. Three options, 10% rate. Pick the largest NPV.

> "NPV is real money today, even though all the cash flows are yet to come in."

blocks.title: What to do with the business
blocks.caption: As set up in lecture, the business is sold at year end in options 2 and 3.

blocks.title: Hire a manager vs sell now
blocks.caption: At 10% the low-stress sale costs you $22,727. Option 3 stops winning above a 20% rate.

blocks.headline: Anthropic's leaked IPO prospectus details steep losses, rapid growth, and a fear that AI could end humanity
blocks.tieIn: Fortune reports an operating loss of $8.06 billion at a company targeting a valuation above $2 trillion. Negative cash flows now, positive NPV only if the story holds. That is the professor's Anthropic example: investors are pricing the future cash flows today, so losing money and being worth trillions can both be true.

blocks.q: You have 12 positive-NPV projects but cash for only some of them. Which do you fund first?
options: The cheapest ones
The ones with the biggest NPV, until the cash runs out
The ones that pay back fastest
The ones you find most interesting
blocks.why: Each NPV is a bucket of money, so you want the biggest buckets. Payback rules can contradict this, which is why NPV is the cleaner guide.

recap: Value is a calculated estimate. Price is what the market charges, and the two only meet in the long run.
NPV is a bucket of cash today: invest when it is positive, reject when it is negative.
PV = FV / (1 + r). The discount rate must match the period of the cash flow.
With limited cash, fund the biggest NPVs first.

quiz.q: In Buffett's definition, intrinsic value equals what?
options: The current market price
The discounted value of cash that can be taken out of a business over its remaining life
The book value on the balance sheet
Last year's profit times ten
quiz.why: Discounted future cash flows is net present value, which is how the course defines value.

quiz.q: What is the present value of $105,000 received in one year at a 7% rate?
A deal has an NPV of -$1,869. What should you do?
options: Take it, the price looks fair
Reject it: it destroys about $1,869 of value in today's dollars
Take it if you can afford it
Wait one year and recompute
quiz.why: Negative NPV means you are giving that much money away, today.

quiz.q: You invest $1M and get $250k a year for four years. The payback rule calls it break-even. What does NPV say at any positive rate?
options: NPV is zero
NPV is positive
NPV is negative
NPV cannot be computed
quiz.why: The cash flows add up to $1M but arrive in the future, so their present value is below $1M.

quiz.q: A riskier version of an investment uses an 11% rate instead of 7%. What happens to the PV of its future cash flow?
options: It rises
It falls
It stays the same
It doubles
quiz.why: A higher rate means a larger discount, so the same future cash is worth less today.

flashcards.back: Price is what the market charges. Value is a calculated estimate (NPV). They equilibrate in the long run, not the short run.
Discounted future benefits minus discounted future costs. A bucket of cash today: positive, invest. Negative, reject.
FV = PV x (1 + r). PV = FV / (1 + r). The same math, run forward or backward.
The base rate, roughly Treasuries and what the Fed moves. Risk premiums and inflation pile on top of it.
Buffett's buffer for being wrong. He may demand a price far below his estimate of value before buying.
Cash flow period and discount rate must match. A 7% annual rate does not discount a cash flow one month away.
